claims.text: In CoFeNiV nanoalloys, d-band filling governs high-temperature structural stability.
In CoFeNiV nanoalloys, d-band filling governs high-temperature chemical stability.
Changing the Co/Fe/Ni/V ratios systematically tunes d-band filling.
Changes in d-band filling induce ordering fluctuations in CoFeNiV.
The proposed ordering fluctuations produce shifts in magnetic signals.
The proposed ordering fluctuations produce local lattice distortions.
Temperature-induced electronic-structure changes alter the strength and nature of interatomic bonding.
Within an optimal composition range, electronic-structure changes induce an ordering transition.
The proposed ordering transition stabilizes CoFeNiV before diffusion-driven degradation dominates.
High-temperature ordering or clustering behavior can vary with temperature and composition in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
CoFeNiV samples at a critical d-band filling will show simultaneous changes in magnetism, lattice parameters, and X-ray absorption signatures between 700 and 1000 °C.
CoFeNiV samples outside the optimal d-band-filling range will exhibit only gradual diffusion-driven changes.
The relevant CoFeNiV compositions traverse a critical valence-electron-concentration threshold.
Outside the stated composition and temperature boundaries, diffusion-dominated processes may obscure the electronic effect.
An inert atmosphere excludes oxidation effects so that temperature and composition are the primary variables.
KKR-CPA can be used to assess structural properties, relative stability, and high-temperature short-range ordering in high-entropy alloys.
The starting CoFeNiV nanoalloys are randomly mixed and crystalline.
A transition occurring independently of d-band filling would falsify the proposed electronic-control mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that all samples are treated under inert atmosphere and that oxidation effects are excluded, whereas the falsification design includes runs under modified oxygen conditions. Those oxygen-control runs are reasonable controls but are exceptions to the claim that all samples are inert.
